title: How money works
blurb: Inflation, interest rates and why time is your best friend.

cards.text: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over time. At 5% inflation, something that cost £100 a year ago costs about £105 now.
It’s measured with a consumer price index: the price of a typical basket of goods and services, checked every month. In the UK the Office for National Statistics does this.
The Bank of England’s target, set by the government, is to keep inflation at 2% a year.
Inflation quietly shrinks what cash can buy. Money kept under the mattress buys a little less each year.

cards.q: The Bank of England’s inflation target is…

points: Inflation is how fast prices rise
It’s measured with a basket of goods

cards.text: The Bank of England sets Bank Rate, the rate it pays banks on money they hold with it. It feeds through to mortgages, loans and savings.
Raising rates makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so people tend to spend less and price rises slow.
Cutting rates does the opposite, encouraging borrowing and spending to support the economy.
Rates are set by the Monetary Policy Committee: nine people who meet eight times a year. The Bank has set rates independently of the government since 1997.

cards.explain: It slows them, by making borrowing and spending less attractive.

points: Bank Rate shapes what borrowing costs
Higher rates cool spending and prices
The MPC decides, eight times a year

cards.text: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest, not just on what you put in. Over time the growth speeds up.
£1,000 growing at 5% a year becomes £1,050 after one year, about £1,629 after 10 years and about £2,653 after 20.
Divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years.
Compounding works against you on debt: unpaid interest is added to the balance, and then that is charged interest as well.

cards.q: By the rule of 72, at 8% money doubles in about…

points: Divide 72 by the rate to find the doubling time

cards.text: Spreading money across many investments means one going wrong doesn’t sink you.
A share is a small slice of a company. A bond is a loan to a company or government that pays interest.
An index fund buys every company in a market index, such as the FTSE 100, usually at low cost.
John Bogle’s Vanguard launched the first index fund for ordinary investors in 1976, following the US S&P 500.
This is general knowledge, not financial advice. Investments can fall as well as rise.

cards.q: What does an index fund do?
opts: Buys everything in a market index
cards.explain: It holds everything in an index, so its return follows the whole market.

points: Don’t put all your eggs in one basket
Shares are slices of companies; bonds are loans
Index funds follow a whole market cheaply
